description: The running spectra of the EGG for one of the vomiting episodes for 30 minutes before and 30 minutes following the report of vomiting is shown. The minutes before vomiting are shown as negative values and the minutes following the vomiting are positive values. Each segment of the spectra overlaps the previous one by 75%, resulting in 51.2 seconds of new data in each segment. The spectra associated with the period of time before vomiting was reported is shown in dark gray and the spectra associated with the period of time after the vomiting was reported is shown in light gray. High amplitude and severe dysrhythmic activity can be observed before the vomiting occurred. The spectral power can be seen equally distributed across the two abnormal rhythms of bradygastria, the slower waves, and tachygastria, the faster waves. After the vomiting episode, a decrease in the EGG amplitude across all frequencies can be observed. At approximately 20 minutes after vomiting, a recovery of the normal 3 cpm gastric slow wave can be seen. Source: Harm DL, Sandoz GR, Stern RM. To generate the arrays, the video camera image was divided into a 64x64 pixel array and the image was sampled at a rate of 60 Hz. At every sample, the position of the rat was determined and the counter in the appropriate occupancy array was incremented. The firing rate array was calculated by dividing, for each pixel, the number of spikes fired when the rat was in the pixel (obtained from the raw files) divided by the number of times the rat occupied that pixel (obtained from the occupancy array). name: Typical Pharmacological Agent Administration and Observation Constraints
parameters: Drug sensitivity
description: Drug sensitivity testing was performed to determine the response of flight crewmembers to each item in the medical kit to preclude allergic reactions and other undesirable side effects in flight. Each Apollo crewmember was tested under controlled conditions to determine his response to medical kit items carried onboard the spacecraft. After a medical history was obtained by a physician regarding the experience of each crewmember with each medication under test, and it had been determined that (1) no adverse reaction had been experienced, and (2) there was no evidence of impaired health at the time of testing, the medication was administered to the astronaut. The crewmember was observed by the physician for an appropriate period of time following administration of the medication and was queried about subjective responses. If positive subjective findings were reported, the test was either repeated with a double-blind placebo method, or an appropriate drug was substituted for which no undesirable side effects had been reported. Individuals were additionally tested for any allergic reaction to the electrode paste. This table lists the medications tested as reported in: Hawkins WR, Zieglschmid JF. Clinical aspects of crew health. In: Johnson RS, Dietlein LF, Berry CA, eds. Biomedical Results of Apollo . Washington, DC: NASA Headquarters; 1975:55-56. NASA SP-368.

name: Interim Study Results from Spaceflight and BedRest
description: Bone loss is a well-documented change during and after long-duration spaceflight. Many types of countermeasures to bone loss have been proposed, including vitamin K supplementation. The objective of this series of studies was to measure change in vitamin K status in response to microgravity under a variety of spaceflight and spaceflight analog (model) conditions, including long-duration spaceflight studies (n?=?15), three bed rest studies (n?=?15, 49, and 24), and a 14-day saturation dive (n?=?6). In crew members who flew 2-6 months on the International Space Station, in-flight and postflight plasma phylloquinone concentrations were unchanged from the preflight mean. Consistent with this finding, urinary ?-carboxyglutamic acid (GLA), a measure of vitamin K-dependent protein turnover, did not change in response to flight. Serum undercarboxylated osteocalcin (%ucOC), a measure of vitamin K function, was generally unchanged in response to flight. Spaceflight findings were corroborated by findings of no changes in phylloquinone, urinary GLA, or %ucOC during or after bed rest in three separate bed rest studies (21-90 days in duration) or after a 14-day saturation dive. The data presented here do not support either a need for vitamin K supplementation during spaceflight or the suggestion of using vitamin K as a bone loss countermeasure in spaceflight.

name: SporeSat2 Ground Experiments – ZeroDay Results
description: This data set contains results from ground experiments using a lab-on-a-chip device designed to measure changes in cellular ion gradients that are induced by changes in gravitational (g) forces. The bioCD detects differential calcium ion concentrations outside of individual cells. Each experimental run is a run of a single bioCD containing 32 wells. Each well is loaded with a single live fern spore (sample) or an intentionally dead spore (negative control) or is left empty (negative control). Each experimental run is as ZeroDay# and this dataset contains ZeroDay4 through ZeroDay13. The device includes sufficient replicates for statistical analysis of the gradients around multiple single cells and around control wells that are empty or include dead cells. In the data presented, the degree of the cellular response correlates with the magnitude of the g-force applied via rotation of the bioCD. The experiments recorded the longest continuous observation of a cellular response to hypergravity made to date, and they demonstrate the potential utility of this device for assaying the threshold of cells' g-force responses in spaceflight conditions. Files are organized into: 1. A Summary of the Variable Conditions for each ZeroDay# experimental run 2. Raw Data from each ZeroDay# run 3. Well images from each BioCD

RNA isolated from 8-hour normal gravity and simulated microgravity S. mutans HARV cultures (n=3 independent experiments per growth condition) was subjected to RNA-seq transcriptome profiling as described in Materials and Methods. RNA isolated from microgravity and normal gravity S. mutans HARV cultures (n=3 each) was converted to cDNA and qRT-PCR was performed using the indicated primers. name: Calbindin-D28k in the rat hypothalamus
parameters: In situ levels; Calbindin, hypothalamus, rat: Immunocytochemistry
description: This excel spreadsheet contains a list of slides that are stored in the investigator's laboratory, along with related treatment information. Sections of hypothalami from STS-56 showed little or no reactivity for calbindin-D28k. This was an unexpected result since calbindin-D28k has previously been described as present in neurons of the ventromedial nucleus, supraoptic nucleus and medial mammillary nucleus of the rat. Because there was weak immunoreactivity for positive control peptides (neuropeptide Y and neurophysin), it is believed that the lengthy storage time in fixative contributed to the diminished immunoreactivity for calbindin-D28k and the control neuropeptides in the hypothalamus. The flight controls as a group showed weaker neurophysin II immunoreactivity than flight animals, however, the flight group exhibited considerable variability in the density of reaction product. Due to weak or absent immunoreactivity in the available tissue specimens, no conclusion can be reached regarding the effect of mg on hypothalamic levels of calbindin-D28k.

description: This graph depicts the time course of symptoms for space motion sickness (SMS) and the range of symptoms that have been recorded on Shuttle crewmembers. With one exception, onset of symptoms (e.g., usually, awareness of motion sensitivity by occasionally vomiting) occurs within minutes to 1-2 hours of exposure to weightlessness. The symptoms progress in intensity over a period of hours to a plateau, which, for a given condition remains stable. There are typically both head (motion sensitivity, malaise, somnolence, lethargy, etc.) and gut (anorexia, vomiting, and nausea) symptoms, although one or the other may predominate. A small subset of crewmembers took medications to prevent SMS only to have the symptoms appear after discontinuation of the medication. Source: Thornton WE, Moore TP, Pool SL, and Vanderploeg J. Clinical characterization and etiology of space motion sickness. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. 1987 September; 58(9 Pt 2):A1-8.

name: Percent Distribution of Spectral Power
description: This graph depicts the percent distribution of spectral power for the three EGG frequency ranges of the gastric myoelectric activity. These three frequency ranges are bradygastria, which is 0.9 to 2.04 cycles per minute (cpm), tachygastria, which is 4.08 to 9.6 cpm and normogastria, which is 2.34 to 3.78 cpm. These three ranges are distinguished in the bars by differing shades of gray. The first two bar graphs show this information for two nausea events experienced by the same crewmember. The percent spectral power relating to 30 minutes and 15 minutes before nausea and 15 minutes, 30 minutes and 45 minutes after nausea are shown. The third bar graph shows the percent spectral power for the vomiting event of another crewmember. Again, 30 minutes and 15 minutes before vomiting and 15 minutes, 30 minutes and 45 minutes after vomiting are shown in the figure. In the first episode of nausea, approximately 60% of the spectral power was associated with abnormal gastric rhythms before nausea was reported. Following the nausea report, the abnormal rhythms increased to approximately 75% of the spectral power then gradually decreased to approximately 45% at 45 minutes following the report. The second episode of nausea gave a percent spectral power associated with abnormal rhythms that was 75 to 80% throughout the recording time of 30 minutes before nausea to 45 minutes after nausea. To generate the arrays, the video camera image was divided into a 64x64 pixel array and the image was sampled at a rate of 60 Hz. At every sample, the position of the rat was determined and the counter in the appropriate occupancy array was incremented. The firing rate array was calculated by dividing, for each pixel, the number of spikes fired when the rat was in the pixel (obtained from the raw files) divided by the number of times the rat occupied that pixel (obtained from the occupancy array). Each bin of the 64x64 bin firing rate map array is a floating point number, composed of 4 bytes. The first 64 entries correspond to the top row of the array, the second 64 entries correspond to the second row, etc. Immediately after the last entry of the last row (entry 4095), the occupancy array starts. name: Typical Pharmacological Agent Administration and Observation Constraints
parameters: Drug sensitivity
description: Drug sensitivity testing was performed to determine the response of flight crewmembers to each item in the medical kit to preclude allergic reactions and other undesirable side effects in flight. Each Apollo crewmember was tested under controlled conditions to determine his response to medical kit items carried onboard the spacecraft. After a medical history was obtained by a physician regarding the experience of each crewmember with each medication under test, and it had been determined that (1) no adverse reaction had been experienced, and (2) there was no evidence of impaired health at the time of testing, the medication was administered to the astronaut. The crewmember was observed by the physician for an appropriate period of time following administration of the medication and was queried about subjective responses. If positive subjective findings were reported, the test was either repeated with a double-blind placebo method, or an appropriate drug was substituted for which no undesirable side effects had been reported. Individuals were additionally tested for any allergic reaction to the electrode paste. This table lists the medications tested as reported in: Hawkins WR, Zieglschmid JF. Clinical aspects of crew health. In: Johnson RS, Dietlein LF, Berry CA, eds. Biomedical Results of Apollo . Washington, DC: NASA Headquarters; 1975:55-56. NASA SP-368.

name: Flight Day 9 Rat 2, Place field maps
parameters: Neural firing rate, rat position
description: Firing rate maps as a function of rat position for individual place cells - illustrate locations at which each neuron fires for Rat 1 on Escher Staircase or Magic Carpet. These files are binary-formatted files that contain two 64x64 pixel arrays of information: the firing rate map for each place cell and a map of position occupancy by the rat during the session. To generate the arrays, the video camera image was divided into a 64x64 pixel array and the image was sampled at a rate of 60 Hz. At every sample, the position of the rat was determined and the counter in the appropriate occupancy array was incremented. The firing rate array was calculated by dividing, for each pixel, the number of spikes fired when the rat was in the pixel (obtained from the raw files) divided by the number of times the rat occupied that pixel (obtained from the occupancy array). name: Orthostatic Stress Procedure Protocol
description: The protocols for the 2 orthostatic stress procedures are shown. The supine LBNP protocol consisted of a 5-minute resting control period, a 5-minute period at each of 3 distinct reduced-pressure levels, and a 5-minute recovery period. The first 5-minute period of reduced pressure included one minute at -8 mm Hg (-11 x 102 N/m2) ) and one minute at -16 mm Hg (-21 x 102 N/m2) ), followed by 3 minutes at -30 mm Hg (-40 x 102 N/m2) ). The 2 short-duration, relatively low levels of reduced pressure were adopted to obtain additional information regarding the responsiveness of lower limb capacitance vessels. The three levels of sequentially applied reduced pressure used were chosen on the basis of previous experience in the JSC Cardiovascular Laboratory (Wolthuis et al., 1970). As reported, the use of an incremental LBNP protocol produced physiological responses for each level of reduced pressure applied and ensured a measurable, quantitative stress response in both the normal preflight and the orthostatically intolerant postflight conditions. The passive stand protocol consisted of a 5-minute resting supine control period followed by a 5-minute passive stand. For the passive stand, the subject leaned against a wall in a relaxed manner with his heels spaced 15 cm (6 in.) away from the wall. Source: Hoffler GW, Johnson RL. name: Duration of Floor Use and Time
parameters: Behavior; Environment
description: This figure shows a temporal analysis which averages the usage over all three weeks. The rates of use for the airlock and Level Two appear to be similar. Because of the exercise function in the airlock, its use by only a single crewmember at a time was extended throughout the waking day with small peaks between 08:00 and 10:00 and between 18:00 and 20:00 as personnel used it for exercise. Level Two usage, however, was almost exclusively in 20-second increments steadily throughout the day û in other words, the amount of time it took for a person to traverse the Level Two landing on the stair while in transit between Levels One and Three. Occasionally, crewmembers would spend slightly larger blocks of time in Level Two in order to check or maintain equipment, but the greatest percentage of use stems from the transit function which was more or less constant throughout the day. The primary focuses of this ground-based experiment were to study and monitor the four subject's daily routines and behavior patterns in the enclosed habitat and apply design techniques to those for long duration space flight missions.

description: Excel worksheets show dates, OD600 measurements and graphs for analysis of growth for strain 1218R and LHM4. Two strain were used, 1218R and LHM4 strain. LHM4 is a derivative of strain 1218R. To produce LHM4 a plasmid was incorporated into the genome of 1218R. The plasmid encodes red fluorescent and kanamycin resistance. Bacteria were grown and experiments performed according to Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi:10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38. For the continuous growth studies, one large volume of OD600 0.0005 culture was prepared from an initiating tube culture and split between two 10 ml HARV: one was subjected to NG and the other to LSMMG. After 4 days the cultures were removed and the OD600 was determined. The statistical difference between the LSMMG and NG cultures was tested by a T-test performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Inc. Gary, NC). To examine culture density during exponential growth, one large volume of OD600 0.002 culture was prepared from an initiating tube culture and split between two 50 ml HARV: one was subjected to NG and the other to LSMMG. Where specified, 3 µg catalase / ml (0.06 U/ ml) (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) was included. Bacteria were grown for ~150 hrs but the HARVs were stopped to remove samples (1 -2 ml). Liquid medium was added to the HARV to replace the removed sample volume (2-4% of the volume) to maintain a low shear environment. Bars represent SEM; * p = 0.001; † p = 0.056. There were no statistically significant differences between BP or cardiac output. No subject experienced hypotension or presyncope during any test. Hemodynamic responses were very similar between flights. . Of note, however, is that mean postflight upright heart rate was significantly higher than the preflight baseline for the control flight (p = 0.001), but was not after the Midodrine flight (p = 0.185) compared with their respective preflight upright heart rates. Orthostatic tolerance was assessed by using the cumulative stress index (CSI; mmHg x minutes) for the LBNP protocol. name: Preflight Rat 3, Place field maps
parameters: Neural firing rate, rat position
description: Firing rate maps as a function of rat position for individual place cells - illustrate locations at which each neuron fires for Rat 3 on Escher Staircase or Magic Carpet. These files are binary-formatted files that contain two 64x64 pixel arrays of information: the firing rate map for each place cell and a map of position occupancy by the rat during the session. To generate the arrays, the video camera image was divided into a 64x64 pixel array and the image was sampled at a rate of 60 Hz. At every sample, the position of the rat was determined and the counter in the appropriate occupancy array was incremented. The firing rate array was calculated by dividing, for each pixel, the number of spikes fired when the rat was in the pixel (obtained from the raw files) divided by the number of times the rat occupied that pixel (obtained from the occupancy array). File format: The file is a binary file containing 32768 bytes. Each byte must be read out in the proper order as follows: First read out the firing rate map array. name: Causes, Symptoms and Treatments of Dental Problems - to be Used with the Contingency Dental Kit
description: This diagram shows the treatment data that would have been used to treat a dental emergency on-orbit during the Skylab missions. This chart shows possible causes of dental problems, their symptoms and treatment procedures. A dental kit was flown on the Skylab missions in the event that a dental emergency arose, and this chart was included with the kit. There were no dental problems requiring the use of this kit, and thus, it was never utilized. Because of the risks of dental problems, the prime and backup crews of all Skylab missions trained for two days in dental procedures at Lackland Air Force Base in Texas. The training included lectures, demonstrations,and supervised clinical procedures, which were performed on volunteer patients, and included complex procedures such as tooth removal. Instruments and medications were provided as the In-flight Medical Support System-Dental. This kit included a manual with line drawings of complete intraoral radiographs of each crewman as well as integratred, illustrated, diagnostic and treatment procedures, one of which is the chart shown in this figure. Other aids included air-to-ground communication with a dentist or surgeon who had intraoral photographs and radiographs, diagnostic casts, complete treatment reacords and knowledge of treatment capabilities of each crewman. name: Apollo Program Immunization Requirements
description: Serological testing was conducted on the Apollo astronauts to determine immunity levels prior to immunizations. The serological tests were performed for tetanus, syphilis, typhoid, mumps, poliomyelitis, rubella, rubeola, and yellow fever. Tuberculin skin tests were also performed. Immunizations against diphtheria, tetanus, typhoid, influenza, poliomyelitis, smallpox, and yellow fever were given to the astronauts. Mumps, rubella, and rubeola immunizations were given if no serological response was obtained. The astronauts’ families were immunized for diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, mumps, poliomyelitis, rubella, rubeola, and smallpox. Other immunizations were provided should the crew members or their families travel to endemic areas. Immunizations were selected after careful review of all known immunizations by NASA medical personnel and a microbiology advisory committee of the National Academy of Sciences. This table lists the immunizations administered in conjunction with the Apollo Program as reported in: Wooley BC, McCollum GW. Flight crew health stabilization program. In: Johnson RS, Dietlein LF, Berry CA, eds. Biomedical Results of Apollo . Washington, DC: NASA Headquarters; 1975:144. Report No.: NASA-SP-368.

Each data set is organized into a variable number of directories (TT0, TT1, etc.) Each directory contains the data recorded from one of the recording “tetrodes” in the rat's brain. The tetrode is a 4-channel electrode that records the activity of a small cluster of neurons. Each channel is labeled x, y, a, or b. There are multiple files within each TT directory. Each file contains the data from one of the cells recorded from that electrode. The number of cells recorded on each electrode varied from 1 to > 10. There are three types of sessions. (1) Data from the animal's run on the Escher Staircase (ES) track, (2) data from the animal's run on the Magic Carpet (MC) track, and (3) data from a baseline (BL) session in which the animal rested quietly in the Rodent Sleeping Pouch. There may be repetitions of each one of these session types. File naming convention: These files are named with the Session type and the neuron number. For example, “ES.cell1” contains the data from Neuron #1 during the Escher Staircase experiment and “BL2.cell5” contains the data from Neuron #5 during the second baseline session. description: Firing rate maps as a function of rat position for individual place cells - illustrate locations at which each neuron fires for Rat 2 on Escher Staircase or Magic Carpet. These files are binary-formatted files that contain two 64x64 pixel arrays of information: the firing rate map for each place cell and a map of position occupancy by the rat during the session. To generate the arrays, the video camera image was divided into a 64x64 pixel array and the image was sampled at a rate of 60 Hz. At every sample, the position of the rat was determined and the counter in the appropriate occupancy array was incremented. The firing rate array was calculated by dividing, for each pixel, the number of spikes fired when the rat was in the pixel (obtained from the raw files) divided by the number of times the rat occupied that pixel (obtained from the occupancy array). name: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria, Bacterium Size Data
description: Size measured from images after growth under LSMMG and normal gravity (NG). Treatment included LSMMG and NG in high-aspect ratio vessels (HARV) on rotating cell culture system (RCCS). For size determination LHM4 strain was used. This is a derivative of strain 1218R. TO produce LHM4 a plasmid was incorporated into the genome of 1218R. The plasmid encodes red fluorescent protein and kanamycin resistance. Bacteria were grown and experiments performed according to Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi:10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38. A portion of the LHM4 culture grown for 4 days in a 10 ml HARV was passed through a 27.5 gauge needle and fixed by the addition of 30 µl 4% paraformaldehyde to 10 µl of culture. Samples were placed at 4°C for at least 24 hrs prior to the measurement of the diameter and length of 50 bacteria using microscopy. The Instat3 program and the Unpaired T-test or the Mann-Whitney test was used to compare the lengths and diameters of the bacterium. Time period of collection November 2014.

name: Significant Twenty-four Hour Urine Biochemistry Changes
description: The biochemical studies on Apollo varied somewhat between missions depending on overall mission objectives. In general, Apollo missions 7, 8, 9 , and 10 were supported in the same manner. Apollo 11, 12, and 14 were characterized by a postflight quarantine and therefore received similar laboratory emphasis. Apollo missions 15, 16, and 17 were supported with an expanded protocol characterized by an increasing number of biochemical studies. The general methods included the withdrawal of 20-ml of venous blood at least three times, approximately thirty, fifteen, and five days before each mission. Similar amounts of blood were withdrawn within two hours after recovery, one day, seven days, and fourteen days later. Fasting blood samples were obtained with the crewmember recumbent and at approximately the same time each day except for the sample immediately after splashdown. The mean of preflight data for each flight (three crewmen, three sample dates) was obtained and the standard deviation of the mean calculated. The mean value of the postflight data (three crewmen, one sample date), the standard deviation and the percent deviation from the preflight level were recorded. parameters: Integral flux; Lineal Energy
description: This graph depicts a comparison of present calculated results with shuttle TEPC data for a 28 degree shuttle flight. The prediction and measured data shown appear to be only within a factor of two near 10 keV/µm but improved over prior results using LET only. The results for both 28 degree and 57 degree flights are consistent in that there is a definite under prediction in the y region below 1 or 2 keV/µm by no more than a factor of 2.3. It appears that these two cases (graphs 4 and 6) will agree with each other if the predicted spectrum for the 28 degree flight is lowered (or the 57 degree is raised) by about 70% or so. This indicates that there might be problems in the orbit-averaged geomagnetic transmission function which is affected by the changes in the earth's magnetic field. The causes for the under prediction below 1-2 keV/µm may be resolved when the indirect delta rays are included in the response model. Source: Shinn JL, Dadwar GD, Xaposos MA, and Wilson JW. description: Hearing tests, also called audiograms or pure-tone air conduction audiometry, were conducted under standard conditions at the health clinic at NASA JSC. The microprocessor audiometer produced pure tone stimuli, recorded subject responses to the sounds and sent the responses to a database. Three audiograms were administered to each of the four LMLSTP subjects. The first occurred at the medical examination required to meet the eligibility requirements, and established baseline readings. The second audiogram occurred within two hours after the subjects egressed the chamber, and the last occurred between 6 and 14 weeks after chamber egress to determine if the hearing threshold had returned to baseline. The audiometer tested each ear independently and started with a training frequency of 1000 cycles per second (Hz). Actual testing proceeded at frequencies of 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000 and 8000 Hz and produced a total of 42 audiogram measurements per subject. Each subject took approximately 12 minutes to complete one audiogram test. An audiogram result of zero indicates that the threshold of hearing is the same as that for an average person without hearing loss. Results above zero indicate hearing loss. Preflight, inflight, and postflight comparisons of Systolic, Diastolic, and Mean Arterial Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, Stroke Volume, and Total Peripheral Resistance at maximum decompression (-50 mmHg). The change in Stroke Volume was significantly greater in flight and postflight compared to preflight (p=0.02) (see *). No other parameters exhibited a significant change, in part due to the large individual variability and small sample size. In fact, the statistical power for all of these comparisons should be considered when drawing any conclusions from these data.

name: Results from Sclerostin Measurements

description: Changes in serum sclerostin and bone turnover markers in healthy adult men undergoing controlled bed rest were determined. Seven healthy adult men (31 ± 3 yr old) underwent 90 days of 6 degree head down tilt bed rest at the University of Texas Medical Branch Institute for Translational Sciences-Clinical Research Center. Serum sclerostin, PTH, vitamin D, bone resorption and formation markers, urinary calcium and phosphorus excretion, and 24-h pooled urinary markers of bone resorption were evaluated before bed rest [baseline (BL)] and at bed rest d 28 (BR-28), d 60 (BR-60), and d 90 (BR-90). Bone mineral density was measured at BL, BR-60, and 5 d after the end of the study (BR+5). Bone mineral density declined significantly (1-2% per month) at weight-bearing skeletal sites. Serum sclerostin was elevated above BL at BR-28 (+29 ± 20%; P = 0.003) and BR-60 (+42 ± 31%; P < 0.001), with a lesser increase at BR-90 (+22 ± 21%; P = 0.07). Serum PTH levels were reduced at BR-28 (-17 ± 16%; P = 0.02) and BR-60 (-24 ± 14%; P = 0.03) and remained lower than BL at BR-90 (-21 ± 21%; P = 0.14), but did not reach statistical significance. Serum bone turnover markers were unchanged; however, urinary bone resorption markers and calcium were significantly elevated at all time points after bed rest (P < 0.01).

description: Spaceflight and bed rest models of microgravity have profound effects on physiological systems, including the cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and immune systems. These effects can be exacerbated by suboptimal nutrient status, and therefore it is critical to monitor nutritional status when evaluating countermeasures to mitigate negative effects of spaceflight. name: Results from Testosterone Measurements
parameters: Cortisol, urine; Testosterone
description: The main objective was to assess testosterone and hormone status in long- and short-duration space flight and bed rest environments and to determine relationships with other physiological systems, including bone and muscle. Blood and urine samples were collected before, during, and after long-duration space flight. Samples were also collected before and after 12- to 14-d missions and from participants in 30- to 90-d bed rest studies. Space flight studies were conducted on the International Space Station and before and after Space Shuttle missions. Bed rest studies were conducted in a clinical research center setting. Data from Skylab missions are also presented. All of the participants were male, and they included 15 long-duration and nine short-duration mission crew members and 30 bed rest subjects. Serum total, free, and bioavailable testosterone were measured along with serum and urinary cortisol, serum dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, and SHBG. Total, free, and bioavailable testosterone was not changed during long-duration space flight but were decreased (P < 0.01) on landing day after these flights and after short-duration space flight. There were no changes in other hormones measured. Testosterone concentrations dropped before and soon after bed rest, but bed rest itself had no effect on testosterone. There was no evidence for decrements in testosterone during long-duration space flight or bed rest.

parameters: Sleep time
description: This graph depicts melatonin and cortisol rhythms in untreated control subjects. Panels A and B reflect melatonin or melatonin sulfate concentrations in saliva or urine, respectively. Cortisol rhythms are shown in Panel C (saliva) and Panel D (urine). Points are means, and error bars SEM, for 15 subjects (14 in Panel A). Normal melatonin rhythms were confirmed in 14 of the 15 control subjects; melatonin concentrations in the saliva of the 15th subject did not change over the course of the day. Melatonin and melatonin sulfate concentrations in saliva and urine, respectively, were low during the day, began to increase at 1800, peaked after midnight, and began to decrease at dawn (panels A and B). Cosinor analysis indicated that the melatonin acrophase (the time at which the peak of a rhythm occurs) was 0130 (saliva) and the melatonin-sulfate acrophase was 0230 (urine). Cortisol concentrations in the control subjects followed a classic diurnal pattern (panels C and D), with concentrations lowest at 2000, remaining low until an abrupt peak around 0600, and decreasing thereafter. Cosinor analysis indicated cortisol acrophases of 0700 (saliva) and 0730 (urine). Individual variations in cortisol concentration were greater than those for melatonin. Source: Whitson PA, Putcha L, Chen YM, and Baker E. Melatonin and cortisol assessment of circadian shifts in astronauts before flight. Journal of Pineal Research. 1995. April; 18(3):141-7.

description: The only measures taken for this phase by the psychological team were basic requirements, selection, and monitoring. In Phase I, selection only consisted of a review of the participant's ability to fulfill the mission, and monitoring was accomplished through informal visits to the chamber/control team to see that things were proceeding well. With the exception of providing the basic psychological requirements, this phase could have been accomplished successfully without any involvement of psychology. The human accommodations incorporated into this first test were rudimentary but sufficient for the duration. Later missions benefited through input from professionals in the physical design and accommodations area. The psychological countermeasures for Phase II were increased over those for Phase I, but were still at a relatively low level due to the brief duration. The development of the mission context was the single most effective and far-reaching psychological act. Source: Holland AW, Curtis K. name: Frequency Analysis Data Recording Sheet
parameters: Sound intensity, decibels
description: The tables show the decibel levels eminating from various pieces of equipment throughout the LMLSTP chamber. The first row of the table shows the level on which the equipment was located. The second row shows the equipment or the location where the decibel reading was taken. Two of the pieces of equipment are the Trace Contaminant Control System (TCCS) and the Four- Bed Molecular Sieve (4-BMS) which adsorbs carbon dioxide. The values in the first column of the table are the frequencies of sound that were monitored. The frequencies are broken down into one third of an octave. The values are given in cps or cycles per second. The K following some of the numerals indicates 1000 cps. Thus, the 8 K is 8000 cps. For each piece of equipment or location the decibels are given for each of these frequencies. At the bottom of the table, in the second to last row, is the A-weighted value that shows the overall decibel level for all frequencies combined for each piece of equipment or location. The comments row shows the distance from the equipment that the docimeter was held. The maps following the tables are the maps of each level of the LMLSTP chamber. They show the locations of the pieces of equipment that were monitored and presented in the tables. Source: Foley T. Unpublished data..

name: Measured GCR dose rate as a Function of Deceleration Potential
parameters: Galactic cosmic rays, dose; Radiation dose rate
description: This graph depicts the combined GCR dose rates measured by the U.S. tissue equivalent proportional counter (TEPC) from March 1995 to January 1998, with data acquired by the Liulin during the last solar cycle, and plotted as a function of the deceleration potential, f(MV). This potential is a parameter that incorporates the solar wind velocity, the interplanetary diffusion coefficient (and their radial dependence), and the extent of the heliospheric boundary from the point of observation. It can be more simply understood as a repulsive potential that cosmic ray particles from the interstellar space have to overcome to reach the point of observation. Source: Badhwar GD. Radiation measurements in low Earth orbit: U.S. and Russian results. Health Physics. 2000. Nov; 79(5):507-14.

Neglecting the target fragments (> 98 keV/µm), and assuming that all of these particles are protons, the investigators inverted the two LET spectra to proton differential energy spectra. Source: Badhwar GD, Kushin VV, Akatov YuA, and Myltseva VA. Effects of trapped proton flux anisotropy on dose rates in low Earth orbit. Radiation Measurements. 1999; June 30 (3): 415-426.

name: Hypercortisolemia alters muscle protein anabolism following ingestion of essential amino acids
parameters: Blood glucose; Cortisol; Essential amino acids; Hydrocortisone sodium succinate; Hypercortisolemia; Insulin; Phenylalanine; Protein balance, net; Protein metabolism, muscle
description: This publication represents the final report for this investigation. Abstract: Debilitating injury is accompanied by hypercortisolemia, muscle wasting, and disruption of the normal anabolic response to food. We sought to determine whether acute hypercortisolemia alters muscle protein metabolism following ingestion of a potent anabolic stimulus: essential amino acids (EAA). A 27-h infusion (80 µg · kg-1 · h-1) of hydrocortisone sodium succinate mimicked cortisol (C) levels accompanying severe injury (>30 µg/dl), (C + AA;n = 6). The control group (AA) received intravenous saline (n = 6). Femoral arteriovenous blood samples and muscle biopsies were obtained during a primed (2.0 µmol/kg) constant infusion (0.05 µmol · kg-1 · min-1) ofl-[ring-2H5]phenylalanine before and after ingestion of 15 g of EAA. Hypercortisolemia [36.5 ± 2.1 (C + AA) vs. 9.0 ± 1.0 µg/dl (AA)] increased postabsorptive arterial, venous, and muscle intracellular phenylalanine concentrations. Hypercortisolemia also increased postabsorptive and post-EAA insulin concentrations. Net protein balance was blunted (40% lower) following EAA ingestion but remained positive for a greater period of time (60 vs. 180 min) in the C + AA group. Thus, although differences in protein metabolism were evident, EAA ingestion improved muscle protein anabolism during acute hypercortisolemia and may help minimize muscle loss following debilitating injury. Source: Paddon-Jones D, Sheffield-Moore M, Creson DL, Sanford AP, Wolf SE, Wolf

A SPE also occurred on November 4, 1997, however the data were completely lost as shown by the absence of measurements in the left-most part of the top panel. The data for the conclusion of the November 6 SPE were also lost. However, during the onset of the November 6 event the Mir Space Station was in the optimal orbital position (i.e. lowest cutoff portions of the orbit) and therefore the measurements reflect the onset and the period of the highest SPE dose contribution. The obvious feature of the SPE event is the presence of high dose maxima at high north and south latitudes, which are comparable to the data experienced during South Atlantic Anomaly crossings. description: This article represents the summarized results of the 17 week horizontal bedrest study. Microgravity, similar to disuse immobilization on earth, causes rapid bone loss. This loss is believed to be an adaptive response to the reduced musculoskeletal forces in space and occurs gradually enough that changes occurring during short duration space flight are not a concern. Bone loss, however, will be a major impediment for long duration missions if effective countermeasures are not developed and implemented. Bed rest is used to simulate the reduced mechanical forces in humans and was used to test the hypothesis that oral alendronate would reduce the effects of long duration (17 weeks) inactivity on bone. Eight male subjects were given daily oral doses of alendronate during 17 weeks of horizontal bed rest and compared with 13 male control subjects not given the drug. Efficacy was evaluated based on measurements of bone markers, calcium balance and bone density performed before, during and after the bed rest. The results show that oral alendronate attenuates most of the characteristic changes in bone that are associated with long duration bed rest and presumably space flight. Source: LeBlanc AD, Driscol TB, Shackelford LC, Evans HJ, Rianon NJ, Smith SM, Feeback DL, Lai D. Alendronate as an effective countermeasure to disuse induced bone loss. J Musculoskelet Neuronal Interact. 2002 Jun;2(4):335-43.

Simulated microgravity impairs vagal baroreceptor-cardiac reflex function and causes orthostatic hypotension. Actual microgravity, however, has been shown to either increase, or not change vagal baroreflex gain. In this study, we tested the null hypothesis that spaceflight does not impair human baroreflex mechanisms. We studied 11 American and two German astronauts before, during (flight days 2-8), and after two, 9- and 10-day space shuttle missions, with graded neck pressure and suction, to elicit sigmoid, vagally mediated carotid baroreflex R-R interval responses. Baroreceptor-cardiac reflex relations were displaced downward on the R-R interval axis in space.
